newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS--Oregon terms may trip Enron, Portland deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS--Oregon terms may trip Enron, Portland deal.

text.p: A $2.1 billion merger between Texas gas giant Enron Corp and Portland General Corp may be short-circuited by Oregon's Public Utility Commission (OPUC), industry analysts said Thursday.
"We don't believe Enron has demonstrated customers would be better off if the merger is approved," Phil Nyegaard, OPUC's financial analysis administrator, told Reuters Thursday.

When Enron and Portland General, the parent of Portland General Electric Co, announced the stock-for-stock deal last July, it was widely touted as a model of convergence between the gas and electricy industries in a deregulated marketplace.
But the companies said late Wednesday they were warned the OPUC staff, citing inadequate advantages for Oregonians, was recommending against approving the merger.
A spokeswoman for Portland General said the companies will await the OPUC staff's report, due April 11, before deciding how to proceed.
But she emphasized "We are following this through to the conclusion," and there are no plans to call off the merger.
Enron said separately it would make its case directly to the OPUC commissioners.
"Hopefully, they will realize that our offer is beneficial to Oregon," an Enron spokesman said earlier Thursday.
The most recent settlement meeting ended last week with the two sides still far apart on how big a cut in Oregonians' electricity bills the merger should provide.

Sources involved in the negotiations told Reuters the talks have foundered amid Enron's lack of experience in dealing with a state regulatory agency and OPUC staff's determination to identify and extract benefits for customers.

One intervenor said the OPUC staff, during the first round of negotiations, identified parts of the Portland utility that ratepayers helped create - such as its wholesale power trading operations - which would be transferred permanently to Enron.
"The premium that Enron was paying indicated they planned to use those assets and expertise to their benefit," the intervenor said.
OPUC analyst Nyegaard said the bulk of the rate cut represents compensation to ratepayers for revenue that would have been generated by the utility even without a merger.
Industry sources said Enron also made a tactical mistake by not negotiating directly with OPUC staff, who were looking to establish the tone of a relationship with a new company.

Instead, the companies held out for a February public hearing before the three-member commission, during which the commissioners made clear that Enron's estimated $3 million per year in unguaranteed cost savings was simply not enough.
Enron and Portland subsequently raised their rate cut offer to $61 million, and reportedly made a one-time offer of $108 million to the staff during last week's meeting.
The OPUC staff originally sought a rate cut of $189.6 million, but trimmed it to $141 million early this month.
Jason Eisdorfer, director of the Citizens' Utility Board of Oregon, said the "secret" nature of the companies' last $108 million offer added to the animosity between the sides.
"You could say that staff turned down the latest offer based on its size, but you could also say the fact that it wasn't an open offer had something to do with it," he noted.
Eisdorfer noted customers and other intervenors are not terribly concerned about whether Portland General ends up merging with anyone, since potential risks may well outweigh any future benefits.

"We are dealing with a new entity that clearly didn't understand the regulatory process. They (Enron) are in another state and there would be gas and electricity transactions that would have to be regulated," he said.

The companies may seek a "contested case hearing" before the commission, if the staff report raises disputes over factual points such as natural gas price forecasts and market share, Portland General spokeswoman Rochelle Lessner said.
